name: Tank Weight Calculator
description: Calculate empty weight of cylindrical steel tanks and vessels plus weight when filled with liquid.

seo.title: Tank Weight Calculator - Steel Vessel Weight (Empty & Filled)
seo.description: Calculate tank weight for steel vessels and pressure tanks. Empty weight + liquid-filled weight, with vertical, horizontal, cone-bottom and dished-head structures plus carbon steel, stainless and aluminum density. Formula explanation, steel density table and sizing examples for fabrication and transport.

formula.expression: pi * diameter * height * thickness * density + (structure == 2 ? 1.0843 * pi * diameter^2 / 4 * thickness * density : structure == 3 ? pi * diameter^2 / 2 * thickness * density : structure == 4 ? 2 * 1.0843 * pi * diameter^2 / 4 * thickness * density : 0) + pi * (diameter/2)^2 * height * liquid_density
formula.explanation: Shell weight: pi x D x H x t x rho (cylindrical wall only, identical for every structure option). End closures are added by structure: option 2 adds one 2:1 elliptical head (1.0843 x pi x D^2 / 4 x t x rho), option 3 adds a 60 degree conical bottom (pi x D^2 / 2 x t x rho), option 4 adds two elliptical heads (2 x 1.0843 x pi x D^2 / 4 x t x rho), option 1 adds nothing. Contents weight: pi x (D/2)^2 x H x rho_liquid, computed on the cylindrical shell volume only. Dimensions in m, thickness converted from mm to m, densities in kg/m3. Nozzles, manways, saddles, skirts and internal supports are not included.

inputs.label: Tank Structure
inputs.hint: 1 = vertical shell only, 2 = vertical + elliptical top head, 3 = vertical + 60 degree cone bottom, 4 = horizontal + two elliptical heads

content.introduction: Calculate the weight of cylindrical steel tanks and pressure vessels — both empty weight and filled weight with liquid. Enter tank dimensions (diameter, height, wall thickness) and material density to get instant weight results in kilograms (kg), with automatic SI unit conversion. This tool is used by engineers and fabricators for steel plate take-off, transportation and crane lift planning, foundation and support load checks, and empty-vs-filled safety evaluation. It supports carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminum, and other vessel materials.

example.description: 3m × 6m × 8mm carbon steel tank + water: shell ≈ 3,550 kg + water ≈ 42,412 kg = ~46,000 kg.

faq.q: How do you calculate the weight of a steel tank?
faq.a: Tank empty weight = pi x D x t x H x rho_steel, where D = diameter, t = wall thickness, H = height, rho_steel = 7850 kg/m3. For a 3m x 6m tank with 10mm wall: W = pi x 3 x 0.01 x 6 x 7850 = 4439 kg.

faq.q: What is the weight of a filled water tank?
faq.a: Filled weight = empty weight + liquid volume x liquid density. A 3m x 6m tank with 10mm steel walls holds ~42,000 liters of water (42,000 kg). Total filled weight = 4,439 + 42,000 = 46,439 kg.

faq.q: How much does a steel tank weigh per square meter?
faq.a: Steel tank wall weight per m2 = thickness(mm) x 7.85 kg/m2/mm. A 10mm steel plate wall weighs 78.5 kg/m2. A 6mm wall weighs 47.1 kg/m2. This quick formula works for flat and cylindrical sections.

faq.q: What steel density should I use for tank weight calculation?
faq.a: Carbon steel: 7,850 kg/m3. Stainless 304: 7,930 kg/m3. Stainless 316: 7,990 kg/m3. Aluminum: 2,700 kg/m3. For most steel tanks, 7,850 kg/m3 is the standard value.

faq.q: Does this calculator include dished heads?
faq.a: It depends on the structure option. Option 1 reports the cylindrical shell only, so heads are excluded. Options 2 and 4 add formed 2:1 elliptical heads, each with a developed area of 1.0843 x pi x D^2 / 4; option 3 adds a 60 degree conical bottom with a developed area of pi x D^2 / 2. Nozzles, manways, saddles, skirts, ladders and internal trays are never included - allow 2-5% of shell weight for these. Use the Pressure Vessel Volume Calculator for head and cone volumes.

faq.q: How do I calculate transport weight for a tank?
faq.a: Transport weight = empty tank weight + liquid weight (if filled) + nozzle/fitting weight (typically 2-5% of shell weight). Always add a 10% safety factor for crane lift planning. Use this calculator for the base shell weight and add accessories separately.

faq.q: How much does a 10,000 litre steel water tank weigh?
faq.a: A 10,000 L (10 m3) cylindrical tank with a 4 mm carbon steel shell has a surface area of roughly 28-32 m2, so the empty steel weight is about 900-1,200 kg (28 m2 x 0.004 m x 7850 kg/m3 ≈ 880 kg plus heads). Filled with water it totals approximately 11,000-11,200 kg.

faq.q: How do I convert tank weight from kg to pounds?
faq.a: Multiply the weight in kg by 2.20462. A 46,000 kg tank = 101,413 lb. For quick estimation, 1 tonne ≈ 2,205 lb.

faq.q: Does the liquid weight affect foundation design?
faq.a: Yes. Foundation and support design must use the filled (operating) weight plus live loads such as seismic and wind. For a 3 m x 6 m water tank, the liquid contributes 42 t compared with only 3.5-4.4 t of steel, so liquid dominates the dead load.

faq.q: How much does a horizontal tank weigh?
faq.a: A horizontal tank weighs the shell plus two heads plus its saddles. For a 3 m diameter, 6 m shell, 8 mm carbon steel vessel the shell is 3,551 kg and two 2:1 elliptical heads add about 963 kg, giving roughly 4,514 kg empty and 46,925 kg full of water on a full-shell basis. Horizontal vessels are usually not filled above the top of the shell, so the real operating weight is a little lower. Select option 4 in the calculator to get this figure automatically.

faq.q: How much does a cone-bottom tank weigh?
faq.a: Add the cone plate to the shell. A 60 degree cone has a developed area of pi x D^2 / 2, twice the plan area, so for a 3 m diameter, 8 mm carbon steel tank the cone weighs about 888 kg against 3,551 kg for the 6 m shell - roughly 25% extra empty weight. Cone-bottom tanks weigh more than flat-bottom tanks of the same capacity because the hopper needs its own support structure as well as the plate.

faq.q: How much does an aluminum tank weigh compared with a steel tank?
faq.a: Aluminum is 2,700 kg/m3 against 7,850 for carbon steel, so the same plate thickness gives 34% of the steel weight - a saving of about two thirds. In practice aluminum needs roughly 1.5 times the wall thickness of carbon steel at equal pressure duty, so the finished saving is closer to 50-55% on empty weight. On the filled weight the difference nearly disappears, because the liquid load is unchanged: 1,386 kg empty versus 4,032 kg empty becomes 43,799 kg versus 46,444 kg total in the 3 m x 6 m example.

content.formula_explanation: Tank weight is calculated as: Empty Weight = Shell Volume x Material Density. Shell Volume = pi x D x thickness x height (the volume of the steel wall). Filled Weight = Empty Weight + Liquid Volume x Liquid Density. Liquid Volume = pi x (D/2 - thickness)^2 x height. The engine converts all inputs to SI base units (meters, kg/m3) and returns weight in kilograms.

sections.heading: Tank Weight Formula Explained
sections.body:
Empty (shell) weight: W_shell = pi x D x t x H x rho, where D = tank diameter (m), t = wall thickness (m, converted from mm), H = shell height (m), rho = material density (kg/m3). The shell weight is the steel volume of the cylindrical wall (surface area pi x D x H times thickness) multiplied by density.
Heads: each flat/elliptical head adds approximately pi x D^2 / 4 x t x rho for a flat head, and roughly 5-10% of shell weight for two 2:1 elliptical heads. This engine reports shell + liquid weight; add head weight separately for total empty vessel weight.
Liquid weight: W_liquid = pi x (D/2)^2 x H x rho_liquid. Filled weight = empty weight + liquid weight. Always use the filled weight for foundation design and the empty weight plus fittings for transport planning.

sections.heading: Worked Example: 3 m x 6 m Carbon Steel Water Tank
sections.body:
Inputs: D = 3 m, H = 6 m, t = 8 mm, carbon steel rho = 7850 kg/m3, water rho = 1000 kg/m3.
Shell surface area = pi x 3 x 6 = 56.55 m2; shell steel volume = 56.55 x 0.008 = 0.452 m3; shell weight = 0.452 x 7850 = 3,551 kg.
Liquid volume = pi x 1.5^2 x 6 = 42.41 m3; water weight = 42,411 kg. Total = 45,962 kg, or about 46.0 tonnes.
If two 8 mm elliptical heads are added (approx 890 kg), the full empty vessel weight is about 4,440 kg and the filled total is about 46,850 kg.

sections.heading: Unit Conversion Reference
sections.body:
Weight: 1 kg = 2.20462 lb; 1 tonne = 1,000 kg; weight in kN = mass (kg) x 9.80665 / 1000. A 46,000 kg tank weighs about 101,400 lb or 451 kN.
Material density (kg/m3): carbon steel 7,850; stainless 304 7,930; stainless 316 7,990; aluminum 2,700; water 1,000; crude oil 850-900; diesel 830-850.
Density conversion: 1 kg/m3 = 0.0624 lb/ft3. Carbon steel in US units is 490 lb/ft3.

sections.heading: Tank Weight vs. Capacity
sections.body: Empty weight is governed by shell surface area and wall thickness, not by capacity alone: a thin-walled large-diameter tank can weigh less than a smaller thick-walled pressure vessel of the same volume. For foundation and support design, use the filled (operating) weight including liquid and fittings; for shipping and lifting, use empty weight plus a 10% rigging safety factor. Related volume tools: Tank Volume Calculator, Tank Capacity Calculator, and Tank Surface Area Calculator provide the geometric inputs used here.

sections.heading: Vessel Structure Options: Vertical, Horizontal, Cone Bottom and Dished Heads
sections.body:
Tank weight depends on how the vessel is closed, not on the shell alone. The shell term (pi x D x H x t x rho) is identical for every structure at the same diameter, height and plate thickness; the difference is the extra plate needed for heads or a conical bottom. Choose the structure in the calculator and the added plate weight is included automatically.
Option 1 - vertical cylinder, flat ends (shell only). The baseline value used by most plate take-offs. Flat ends are normally formed by the floor or roof structure rather than a dished head, so no head plate is added. Use it for open-top tanks, tanks standing on a concrete slab, and quick fabrication estimates.
Option 2 - vertical cylinder with a 2:1 elliptical top head. A formed head with depth equal to one quarter of the diameter. The developed head area is taken as 1.0843 x pi x D^2 / 4, so for a tank with H = 2D the head plate is about 13.6% of the shell plate weight, and the share grows quickly for squat, large-diameter tanks.
Option 3 - vertical cylinder with a 60 degree conical bottom. A self-draining hopper bottom. At 60 degrees from horizontal the cone slant length equals the diameter, so the developed area is pi x D^2 / 2, twice the plan area. For H = 2D the cone plate is roughly 25% of the shell plate weight, and the cone holds about 0.227 x D^3 m3 below the shell.
Option 4 - horizontal cylinder with two 2:1 elliptical heads. The standard horizontal storage vessel, with both ends formed, so twice a single head plate is added (about 27% of shell plate at H = 2D). Saddles, nozzles, manways and the reinforcing pads around them are not included.
Flat-ended and dished-head vessels of the same volume do not weigh the same: dished heads use less plate than a flat end of equal pressure rating but add depth and shop hours, so for small tanks flat ends often win on cost while dished heads win on pressure capability.

sections.heading: Material Selection: Carbon Steel, Stainless Steel and Aluminum
sections.body:
Plate weight scales linearly with density. For 1 mm of plate, weight per square metre is density / 1000: carbon steel 7.85 kg/m2 per mm, stainless 304 7.93, stainless 316 7.99, aluminum 2.70. The same 3 m x 6 m x 8 mm shell weighs 3,551 kg in carbon steel, 3,587 kg in 304 stainless (about 1% more) and only 1,221 kg in aluminum (66% less).
Stainless steel is chosen for product contact, hygiene and corrosion allowance, not for weight saving. The 1% density penalty is negligible against the cost step, and stainless vessels are often built in a heavier gauge than carbon steel because allowable stress falls at elevated temperature.
Aluminum cuts empty weight by two thirds, which matters for transport, lifting and tanks carried on light structures. The saving is partly given back in service, because aluminum needs roughly 1.5 times the wall thickness of carbon steel at equal pressure duty once the lower modulus and lower allowable stress are accounted for.
Contents weight is unaffected by shell material: it depends only on volume and liquid density - water 1,000 kg/m3, diesel 830-850, crude oil 850-900, 98% sulfuric acid 1,840, saturated brine 1,200. Use the filled weight for foundation and support design and the empty weight plus fittings for transport.

sections.heading: Worked Examples: How Structure and Material Change the Weight
sections.body:
All examples use D = 3 m, H = 6 m shell, t = 8 mm plate and water at 1,000 kg/m3, so only structure and material change between cases.
Option 1, carbon steel: shell = pi x 3 x 6 x 0.008 x 7850 = 3,551 kg; water = pi x 1.5^2 x 6 x 1000 = 42,412 kg; total 45,963 kg, of which the empty weight is just 7.7%.
Option 2, carbon steel with a 2:1 elliptical top head: head plate = 1.0843 x pi x 3^2 / 4 x 0.008 x 7850 = 481 kg; empty weight 4,032 kg; total 46,444 kg.
Option 3, carbon steel with a 60 degree conical bottom: cone plate = pi x 3^2 / 2 x 0.008 x 7850 = 888 kg; empty weight 4,439 kg; total 46,851 kg. The cone is the heaviest of the single-end options because its developed area is twice the plan area.
Option 4, horizontal carbon steel with two elliptical heads: head plate = 2 x 481 = 963 kg; empty weight 4,514 kg; total 46,925 kg on a full-shell basis, which is conservative because a horizontal vessel is rarely filled to the centreline of the top head.
Material comparison on option 2: the same geometry in 304 stainless gives 4,073 kg empty and 46,485 kg total; in aluminum it gives 1,386 kg empty and 43,799 kg total. The liquid load dominates every case, so shell material choice moves total weight by only a few percent while it moves empty weight by a factor of three.

sections.heading: How to Check the Result Before Fabrication
sections.body:
Use the weight as a plate take-off cross-check, not as a bill of materials. Multiply the shell area (pi x D x H) by plate thickness and density, then add heads, nozzles, manways, reinforcing pads, ladders, platforms, insulation supports and any internal trays. Nozzle and manway assemblies typically add 2-5% of shell weight on small vessels and rather less on large storage tanks.
For lifting, add a rigging factor: 10% is the usual allowance for a single crane lift with certified slings, and the empty weight plus rigging factor is what the crane chart should be read against. For transport, use empty weight plus saddles or transport frame, and check axle loads against the road limit rather than against the tank weight alone.
For foundation design, use the filled operating weight plus snow, wind and seismic components. A 46 tonne water load on a 3 m diameter tank is a 65 kPa bearing pressure on the base ring, which is normally well inside a reinforced concrete slab but must be checked against the local soil capacity when the tank sits on grade.
Cross-check geometry with the Tank Volume Calculator for capacity, the Tank Surface Area Calculator for plate area, and the Pressure Vessel Volume Calculator for head and cone volumes. The Cylinder Volume Calculator and Steel Weight Calculator cover the simpler cases.
